contrary_evidence: Visible Hormuz traffic remains severely below recent averages despite partial Saudi export-logistics relief, so the energy shock is not resolved.
Alternative Saudi and UAE routes can bypass only part of normal Hormuz volumes; redundancy reduces but does not eliminate route exposure.
Refined-product markets, especially diesel, remain tight; lower crude prices therefore do not imply equivalent relief in transport or industrial fuel costs.
Public bank forecasts differ on the timing of the next Fed hike, so one Goldman Sachs forecast change cannot establish broad institutional consensus.
limitations: Kpler/Reuters Hormuz observations are preliminary snapshots with non-comparable cutoffs and/or classification states; AIS-dark traffic can be omitted, so they cannot support a precise day-over-day throughput series.
The Tanker War is used only as a historical mechanism comparison; different actors, capabilities and political conditions prevent treating it as a forecast template for the current conflict.

The fiscal and household pass-through of an energy shock varies materially by country according to fiscal buffers, subsidies, taxes, exchange rates and household consumption patterns; the report appropriately states the channel conditionally rather than as a uniform observed effect.
Several market prices are intraday observations rather than official closes and are time-sensitive.
The energy-relief mechanism depends partly on expected restoration of Saudi pipeline capacity and therefore remains less certain than the observed monetary-policy change.
notes: Revision 3 is a contextual-depth revision of public revision 2. It adds a mechanism-relevant Tanker War/Operation Earnest Will historical anchor and an explicit fiscal/household transmission channel, with society added as a dimension. The core quantitative market thesis, scenarios and institutional-consensus treatment remain materially unchanged. Approval is valid only for the exact pending and staged-source blob SHAs recorded here.

qa_fixes_applied: Downgraded institutional consensus state from Broadening to Unclear because only Goldman Sachs had a sufficiently attributable dated house-view change; Fed projections and market pricing are no longer counted as institutional research signals.
Reconciled Reuters/Kpler Hormuz observations and stopped treating incompatible preliminary snapshots as a continuous day-over-day series.
Recalculated energy-relief confidence so the thesis relies on Saudi alternative export loadings, expected East-West pipeline restoration and observed crude-price easing.
Reworked the public opening so it states the analytical finding directly instead of exposing Executive Assessment, Regime, Observed Fact, Inference and Confidence as template fields.
Replaced generic or internal-facing headings with finding-led headings, localized Portuguese terminology, removed exposed internal classification labels and reduced repeated QA/process language.
Condensed the repeated Hormuz caveat to preserve the methodological limitation without repeating the revision history across multiple sections.

Integrated a mechanism-relevant historical anchor from the 1980s Tanker War and Operation Earnest Will to explain why route security, insurance and vessel behavior affect effective transport capacity without using history as a prediction template.

Added the fiscal and household transmission channel linking prolonged Gulf energy disruption to public spending, real incomes and employment-sensitive sectors, making the social dimension materially explicit.
